title: Maggots: Good For Healing Wounds, Turns Out
summary: Josh and Chuck explain maggot debridement therapy, the medical use of live, sterile green blowfly larvae to clean dead tissue from open wounds. They cover its ancient roots, the 16th-century surgeon Ambroise Paré, Dominique Jean Larrey's Egyptian expedition observations, the Civil War use by John Forney Zacharias, William S. Baer's World War One work and sterile maggots at Johns Hopkins, the mid-century boom and later decline, and the 1990s revival by Ronald Sherman. They explain the three cleaning mechanisms (mechanical debridement by spines, digestive secretions, antimicrobial and biofilm destruction), the FDA device classification, treatment cycles, and studies showing faster debridement than standard care, including MRSA cases. They also discuss diabetic foot ulcers and amputation risk, and encourage patients to ask doctors about the therapy and check insurance coverage through the BTER Foundation. The episode closes with a listener email about settled science in climate discussions.

segments.title: Opening banter and content warning
segments.summary: Hosts joke about the show's production setup, issue a warning about eating during the episode, and introduce maggot therapy as the topic.

segments.title: Definition and early history of maggot therapy
segments.summary: Maggot debridement therapy is defined as placing live fly larvae in open wounds. The hosts trace its use in ancient cultures and early Western medicine, including Ambroise Paré's skull wound observation and Dominique Jean Larrey's Egyptian expedition notes.

segments.title: Civil War, World War One, and sterile maggots
segments.summary: John Forney Zacharias used maggots deliberately during the Civil War. William S. Baer used them in World War One and later pioneered sterile maggots at Johns Hopkins. Use boomed in the 1930s and 1940s, then declined with new antiseptics and germ theory.

segments.title: Revival in the 1990s and modern status
segments.summary: Maggot therapy declined in the mid-twentieth century and was revived in the 1990s by Ronald Sherman and Edward Pector. Sherman was among the first licensed to produce sterile maggots as medical devices, and John Church brought the therapy to the UK.

segments.title: Diabetic ulcers, amputation, and advocating for therapy
segments.summary: Diabetes-related nerve damage and poor circulation can lead to ulcers, infection, osteomyelitis, and amputation. The hosts suggest patients ask doctors about maggot therapy before amputation, and mention the BTER Foundation and insurance coverage issues.

segments.title: How maggots clean wounds
segments.summary: Maggots clean wounds through mechanical debridement from their spines, digestive secretions that liquefy dead tissue, and antimicrobial action. Their secretions also destroy biofilm, and the FDA classifies them as a device. Each maggot removes about 25 milligrams of necrotic tissue in a day.

segments.title: Pain, treatment cycles, and clinical studies
segments.summary: The hosts discuss pain during treatment, the use of green blowfly larvae, application density, the 48 to 72 hour treatment cycle, and studies showing faster debridement than standard care, including MRSA cases.

segments.title: Listener mail on settled science
segments.summary: A listener writes that science is never settled, responding to Josh's earlier remark about climate change. Josh says he was using a literary device.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener feedback through social media and email and point listeners to the website.
